Article content: {"cover_media":"3_2087126125696720896","entities":{"urls":[{"text":"https://nyk.dev/#newsletter"},{"text":"https://t.me/+GJ-FEpzcZrtmMTky"},{"text":"https://nyk.dev/#newsletter"},{"text":"https://t.me/+GJ-FEpzcZrtmMTky"}]},"media_entities":["3_2087125745973841920","3_2087125817142702080","3_2087125889377095680","3_2087125975628722176"],"plain_text":"Almost-right code is more expensive than wrong code.
Wrong code usually fails fast. AI-generated code that is almost right survives the first glance, passes the smoke test, and breaks where you were not looking.
Stack Overflow's 2025 survey of 31,476 developers shows the scale of that cost. 66% reported AI solutions that were almost right, but not quite - the most common frustration in the results.
Here is the check I run before I ship it, and what it caught.
 
Sitting directly beneath it, from the same question set: 45.2% say debugging AI-generated code is more time-consuming.
Read those two together and the shape of the problem changes. The 45.2% debugging figure is the cost hiding inside the 66% frustration figure.
This is not an argument for using these tools less. Adoption in the same survey is 84% using or planning to use AI tools, up from 76% the year before, with 51% of professional developers using them daily. The tools are in the workflow and they are staying there.
It is an argument that "I reviewed it" is not a check. Here is what I run instead, and what it caught.
The trust numbers, and why I am not leading with them
The most quotable statistic here is the trust collapse, and I am deliberately not building on it, because Stack Overflow's own two publications about this survey do not agree.
 
The survey results page reports that 33% somewhat or highly trust the accuracy of AI tools, while 46% actively distrust it. Only 3% fall into the highest trust band, across 33,244 respondents.
The Stack Overflow blog post about the same survey states that trust in the accuracy of AI has fallen from 40% in previous years to 29% this year.
Those are different numbers for what reads like the same measure, published by the same organization about the same survey. The discrepancy may come from a different question or population, but Stack Overflow does not specify which. Choosing an explanation would mean inventing one for a cleaner sentence.
So the figure I use is the one carrying a stated sample size on the primary results page: 46% actively distrust the accuracy, against 33% who trust it. Distrust outweighs trust by roughly half again. That is enough to make the point without resting on a number I cannot reconcile.
One number the two publications broadly agree on is the direction of sentiment: positive favorability sits at 60% this year, down from above 70% in the two prior years. Both sources record a decline of roughly the same size. Where they diverge is the precise trust figure, which is the one people quote.
I am flagging this because it is the exact failure mode the rest of this article is about. An almost right statistic.
Developers already know, and their fallback is a person
The survey has one more figure that reframes the whole problem. When developers
do not trust an AI answer, 75.3% say they would still ask another person.
 
That is the correct instinct and it does not scale. Asking a person is a good
check because a person can refuse, can say "that command does not exist", and
can be specific about why. It is a bad check because it is unavailable at 2am,
inconsistent between reviewers, and expensive enough that you skip it precisely
when you are under the deadline that made you reach for the tool.
The distribution underneath the trust numbers explains why the fallback gets
used so often. Only 3% of respondents highly trust AI accuracy. Among
professional developers the gap is starker still: 2.7% highly trust against
19.7% who highly distrust. Almost nobody is confident, and yet 51% of
professional developers use these tools daily and 84% use or plan to, up from
76% the year before.
That is the actual state of practice: heavy use, low confidence, and a human
verification step that is the first thing dropped under pressure. A mechanical
check is not a replacement for the colleague. It is the part of the colleague's
job that can be made to run every time.
What a check has to do that a review does not
Reading generated code tells you whether it looks correct. That is a genuinely useful signal, and it is not the same as verification, because the failure mode here is specifically output that looks correct.
A check has to be a thing that can fail. Concretely, it needs three properties.
It must be mechanical - it produces the same verdict on the same input, whether you are tired. It must be specific - it names what is wrong and where, rather than returning a general impression. And it must be capable of refusing - if it can only advise, it will be overridden on the day it matters, which is the day you are shipping late.
Most of what people call review fails the third one.
A plausible command is still a false command
Consider an AI-generated setup guide that recommends a handful of plausible commands. The product is real. The syntax looks consistent. Each command sounds like something the tool should support.
A read-through cannot settle whether those commands exist. The installed binary can. Extract each invocation, compare it with the tool's actual help output, and refuse the guide if any command or flag is missing.
That distinction matters because plausibility is exactly what makes almost-right output expensive. Obvious nonsense is discarded. A convincing command reaches a terminal.
That is the whole design principle. Do not ask whether the output looks right. Ask the system that would know.
The four checks, in the order they run
1. Does the thing you named exist?
Check every command and flag against the tool installed in the target environment. If the checker cannot reach the tool, the result is not "valid". It is "unverifiable", and the output should stop there.
A checker that shrugs and passes is worse than no checker, because it produces the paperwork of verification without the verification. A checker can also refuse for the wrong reason: a restricted shell may not inherit the same PATH as an interactive terminal, making an installed tool appear absent.
The lesson is not that fail-closed is insufficient. It is that a gate reporting "I cannot check this" deserves the same suspicion as a gate reporting "this is fine", because both can be produced by a broken gate.
2. Does every number have a receipt?
Any figure that reaches the reader must name where it came from and when it was measured. Not a citation in the general direction of a source - the specific value, the specific source, the date it was read.
That is what makes conflicting figures visible. When two receipts disagree, preserve the disagreement instead of silently choosing the cleaner number.
3. Do the claims still match the text?
Store every load-bearing claim with the exact sentence it certifies. If that sentence changes afterward - even by one meaningful character - the claim must be reviewed and certified again.
That sensitivity is inconvenient by design. The alternative is a ledger that appears current while certifying language the reader can no longer see.
4. What did you decide not to say?
The last check is human judgment, and it is the one worth keeping if only one can survive.
Write down the limitations and objections raised during review. Not a generic disclaimer. Name which population a number describes, what a measurement excludes, which framing was challenged, and what evidence would change the conclusion.
The objections are often more useful than the supporting notes. They preserve the arguments against the conclusion while those arguments are still easy to remember.
What this costs, honestly
This is slower. Not dramatically, but noticeably: the checks add a pass that often fails, and each failure is work.
It is also incomplete. The command checker verifies that a command exists, not that it behaves as described. The receipt check verifies that a number has a source, not that the source is sound. As the trust-figure conflict demonstrates, a fully sourced figure can still be contested. Claim hashes prove that a sentence has not drifted, not that it was ever true.
None of these checks can make weak material good. Their job is narrower: stop unsupported material from shipping. That lower bar is still valuable.
The checks are code, and code has bugs. Test the gate with known-good and known-bad examples. A verification step that is never challenged is another assumption wearing a green badge.
The part worth keeping
The survey's top complaint is not that AI writes bad code. It is that it writes almost right code - and 45.2% of developers pay for that in debugging time.
Reading alone rarely catches almost-right output because such output is designed to survive a read. Use systems that can answer four questions: Does this command exist? Does this number have a source? Does this claim still match the sentence? Which limitations remain unstated?
The operating rule is simple: route each claim to the system best equipped to refuse it. Appearance is not evidence.
